design-pub-sub-messaging-platform.summary: Design a durable partitioned event log with independent consumer groups. Producers append events; consumers advance their own offsets and can replay retained history. Ordering is per partition, and end-to-end correctness depends on how consumer output is committed, not merely on a broker claiming exactly-once support.
clarifyingQuestions: Is ordering required per key, per partition, or globally, and can keys be redistributed?
What does a producer acknowledgment guarantee under disk, node, and regional failure?
How long can consumers lag, and do their external effects need transactional checkpointing or idempotency?

deepDives.title: Acknowledgment, replication, and leader epochs
paragraphs: A broker append must define when it becomes committed and what an acknowledgment survives. Replication count, in-sync replica rules, disk persistence, and leader election all participate. 'Replicated' does not automatically mean every acknowledged record survives every correlated power or regional failure.

Fence obsolete leaders with epochs and avoid promoting replicas that lack acknowledged committed data when the durability contract forbids loss. During a partition, choosing availability through an unclean promotion is a conscious data-loss trade-off, not a transparent recovery mechanism.

Producer identity and sequence can deduplicate retries within their supported scope. State how producer restarts and epochs behave, and whether transactions span partitions. Broker-side deduplication prevents some duplicate appends but cannot undo an unrelated external effect already performed by a consumer.
deepDives.invariant: An acknowledged committed record is not silently discarded by a promotion policy that claims to preserve that durability level.

followUp.question: Does waiting for multiple replicas prove zero data loss under every failure?
followUp.answer: No. It depends on persistence, which replicas may be promoted, and the assumed failure model. Correlated loss of all acknowledged copies still loses data. State the replication and election rules together with the supported recovery point objective.

deepDives.title: Consumer effects and rebalance fencing
paragraphs: A consumer that commits its offset before applying the effect risks loss; one that applies the effect first risks duplication after a crash. Store the effect and checkpoint atomically in one sink where possible, or make the effect idempotent using a durable event identity.

Parallel processing creates another trap: committing the highest completed offset can skip earlier unfinished records. Advance only a contiguous completed watermark for the partition, and bound in-flight work. Preserve per-key ordering if the application relies on it rather than assuming the broker's ordered fetch implies ordered effects.

During rebalance, an old worker may still be processing after a new owner starts. Stop and drain it where possible, and fence commits or sink effects using a generation/ownership token. Exactly-once claims are scoped to supported transactional boundaries; arbitrary HTTP calls and emails still require their own recovery contract.
deepDives.invariant: A committed consumer checkpoint never skips unfinished required effects, and obsolete owners cannot commit as the current partition owner.

followUp.question: What is missing from 'Kafka is exactly once, so our payment call is exactly once'?
followUp.answer: The external payment processor is outside the broker transaction. Use stable payment-attempt identity, provider idempotency, and reconciliation. Transactional broker output and offsets do not atomically include an arbitrary network side effect.

deepDives.title: Partition sizing, retention, and backpressure
paragraphs: Partitions provide parallelism but preserve order only inside their boundaries. A single hot ordering key remains hot after adding partitions unless the application changes that key's semantics. Benchmark bytes, batch sizes, compression, disk bandwidth, and consumer work rather than treating partition count as a universal throughput setting.

Retention is a recovery window. If a consumer falls behind beyond retained history, replay becomes impossible without an external archive or snapshot. Track lag in time and bytes as well as record count, because a million tiny messages and a million large messages imply different recovery costs.

Protect brokers from producers and consumers through quotas, bounded batches, and fetch limits. Poison records need explicit quarantine and replay ownership, not an endless retry loop that blocks an entire ordered partition. Schema evolution must let old and new consumers coexist during rollout and historical replay.
deepDives.invariant: The service either retains the history promised for recovery or explicitly reports that a consumer must resynchronize from another source.

followUp.question: Why can increasing partitions break application behavior?
followUp.answer: A key may map to a different partition while old records remain in the previous one, changing how ordering is observed. Plan key migration and consumer compatibility, and do not assume higher parallelism preserves the same cross-partition ordering contract.

signals.name: Durability health
signals.measure: Track in-sync replicas, leadership changes, rejected stale epochs, and commit latency.
signals.response: Stop unsafe promotions and restore replicas before relaxing acknowledgment guarantees.

signals.name: Consumer recovery window
signals.measure: Measure time/byte lag, oldest retained offsets, rebalance duration, and contiguous checkpoint progress.
signals.response: Scale useful consumer work, repair poison-record handling, and trigger archive/snapshot recovery before history expires.

signals.name: Capacity and fairness
signals.measure: Monitor per-partition bytes, hot keys, disk headroom, producer quotas, and fetch amplification.
signals.response: Throttle noisy tenants and rebalance with ordering-aware migration rather than only increasing partition count.

security: Use authenticated encrypted clients and topic/group ACLs, separating producer, consumer, and cluster-administration permissions.
Bound message size and decompression work, and prevent tenant-controlled keys from monopolizing partitions or metadata resources.
Classify retained payloads and enforce deletion/retention policy across replicas and archives without assuming log compaction immediately removes every copy.
validation: Kill leaders around acknowledgments and prove the configured durability/election contract under the stated failure model.
Crash and rebalance consumers between effects and checkpoints, including out-of-order parallel completion and stale-owner writes.
Replay old schemas and poison records in a bounded test environment; canary partition and retention changes with lag and disk-capacity gates.

prerequisites: Append-only logs, replication, and leader epochs
Partitions, offsets, consumer groups, and idempotent sinks

functional: Create topics and append keyed events with acknowledgment options.
Let independent consumer groups subscribe, checkpoint, and replay within retention.
Preserve order within a partition and recover from broker or consumer failures.
nonFunctional: Illustrative target: sustain 100,000 1-KB events/s with batching.
Define durability against a stated number of broker failures before acknowledging writes.
Scale consumers without losing partition ownership or silently skipping records.
outOfScope: A total order across every partition and topic.
Exactly-once arbitrary HTTP calls or database side effects without destination cooperation.

assumptions: 100,000 events/s, 1 KB/event, and seven days of retention.
Replication factor three; assume no compression for a conservative payload estimate.

estimates.label: Ingress
estimates.calculation: 100,000 x 1,000 B = 100 MB/s client ingress; two replica copies add roughly 200 MB/s of payload replication.
estimates.implication: Budget consumer egress separately, batch writes, and benchmark broker disk and network throughput.

estimates.label: Retention
estimates.calculation: 100 MB/s x 86,400 x 7 = 60.48 TB raw; three copies = 181.44 TB before indexes and headroom.
estimates.implication: Retention and replication multiply cost. Tiered storage and compression can help, but replay performance must still satisfy the recovery objective.

api.purpose: Route a key to a partition, append, and acknowledge at the requested durability level. Producer sequence metadata can deduplicate eligible retries.
Pull a bounded batch. Define behavior for an offset older than retention rather than silently inventing missing history.
Advance progress only for the current consumer-group generation; fence consumers that lost partition ownership.

dataModel.fields: topic, partition, offset, key, timestamp, schemaId, payload
dataModel.notes: Offsets are partition-local positions. Event keys choose the ordering and load-distribution boundary.

dataModel.fields: leader, replicas, inSyncReplicas, epoch, retentionPolicy
dataModel.notes: Coordinate leader election and fence obsolete leaders. Durability depends on acknowledgment and minimum-replica configuration.

dataModel.fields: groupId, partition, nextOffset, generation
dataModel.notes: Different groups replay independently. Commit semantics must align with the processing output's durability.

architecture.diagram:
flowchart TD
 Producer[Producer with retries] --> Leader[Partition leader]
 Leader --> Log[(Segment log)]
 Leader --> Replica[(Follower replicas)]
 Metadata[Metadata quorum] -.-> Leader
 Leader --> GroupA[Consumer group A]
 Leader --> GroupB[Consumer group B]
 GroupA --> SinkA[(Idempotent output store)]
 GroupB --> SinkB[(Independent output store)]
 GroupA --> Offsets[(Group offsets)]

flows.name: Append durably
steps: Resolve topic metadata, hash the event key to a partition, and send a batch to its current leader.
The leader appends records and replicates them. With all-in-sync acknowledgments, require the configured minimum in-sync replicas before success.
Return assigned offsets. If the response is lost, retry using supported producer identity and sequence numbers.
On leader change, refresh metadata and respect leader epochs; do not acknowledge writes from an obsolete leader.

flows.name: Process and replay
steps: A group coordinator assigns partitions to consumers; one group member normally processes a partition at a time.
Fetch from the committed nextOffset and process a bounded batch, preserving required order within each partition.
Commit output durably before advancing the offset for at-least-once processing; a crash between those steps causes replay.
Deduplicate effects in the sink or atomically store output and checkpoint where possible. On rebalance, fence old owners and resume from the last committed position.

decisions.choice: Key events by the entity whose order matters, such as account or conversation.
decisions.tradeOff: Hot entities concentrate load. Adding partitions can remap keys, so strict ordering across repartitioning needs a migration plan.

decisions.choice: Let consumers request batches and control their own pace.
decisions.tradeOff: Pulling makes backpressure and replay explicit, but consumers must monitor lag and retention before slow processing turns into irreversible data loss.

decisions.choice: Use supported transactions for compatible read-process-write pipelines and idempotent or transactional sinks elsewhere.
decisions.tradeOff: Broker transactions do not make an unrelated email provider or HTTP endpoint transactional. The claim must name the boundaries it covers.

failureModes.scenario: A consumer crashes after writing output but before committing its offset.
failureModes.handling: Expect replay and deduplicate by event identity or transactionally bind output and checkpoint. Committing before output instead risks data loss.

failureModes.scenario: A slow consumer falls behind the retention window.
failureModes.handling: Alert on lag age relative to retention, scale processing or isolate poison events, and recover from an archive if available. Resetting offsets discards data and must be explicit.

failureModes.scenario: Replication falls below the configured minimum.
failureModes.handling: Reject or pause durable writes rather than silently weakening the contract. Monitor in-sync replica count, under-replicated partitions, disk space, produce latency, and rebalance frequency.

selfCheck.question: Why can adding consumers stop improving throughput?
selfCheck.answer: Within one consumer group, useful parallelism is usually bounded by the partition count, and a hot partition still has one ordered processing lane. More idle consumers cannot split a partition's strict ordering requirement without changing the workload design.

selfCheck.question: When should the offset be committed relative to writing output?
selfCheck.answer: Committing after durable output gives at-least-once processing because a crash may replay completed work. Commit output and offset atomically where supported, or deduplicate effects. Committing the offset first creates a crash window that loses output.

selfCheck.question: Does producer idempotence make sending a payment request exactly once?
selfCheck.answer: No. Producer idempotence addresses eligible duplicate appends to the broker. A consumer can still replay and call a payment API again; the payment operation needs its own durable idempotency contract and reconciliation strategy.

design-search-autocomplete.summary: Design a low-latency prefix-suggestion service with a separate indexing pipeline. Serving every keystroke from raw query logs is too expensive, so prepare top suggestions offline or incrementally and publish versioned indexes. Popularity, language, privacy, and freshness determine what belongs in the index; a trie alone does not solve those product decisions.
clarifyingQuestions: Are suggestions global, locale-specific, personalized, or limited to an authorized product catalog?
How fresh must trending suggestions be, and how quickly must unsafe or private phrases disappear?
What prefix lengths, languages, typo tolerance, and response latency are required?

deepDives.title: Precomputed candidates and bounded serving
paragraphs: Do not aggregate raw query history for every keystroke. Build bounded top candidates per normalized prefix or use a compact trie/FST-style index with a completion mechanism. Store display text separately from matching form so case folding, accents, and locale policy do not corrupt the rendered suggestion.

Choose partitioning with short hot prefixes in mind. Locale or prefix ranges can help, but popular first letters remain skewed. Cache common results and merge a bounded candidate set when queries span shards. Enforce a serving deadline and output limit so typo expansion cannot turn a tiny request into an unbounded search.

Client behavior is part of the load model. Debounce where appropriate, handle composition input, cancel obsolete requests, and discard replies for older query generations. Server correctness does not prevent a late response for an earlier prefix from replacing the current suggestions in the client.
deepDives.invariant: Each response has a bounded candidate and latency budget and corresponds to the intended normalized query and index version.

followUp.question: Why is building a trie not a complete autocomplete design?
followUp.answer: It addresses prefix lookup, but not ranking, language normalization, fresh updates, privacy filtering, hot-prefix load, or stale client responses. Those policies determine what candidates belong in the index and how they can be served safely.

deepDives.title: Index publication and trending updates
paragraphs: Build a candidate index from a validated corpus or aggregate stream, version its schema and scoring rules, and test it before publication. Readers should atomically switch a manifest or alias to a complete index. Publishing shards independently without a compatibility rule can mix vocabulary, score, and metadata versions.

Combine a stable baseline with a small recent-trend overlay when freshness justifies it. Deduplicate candidates across layers and define how scores are comparable. A trend spike should not require rebuilding the entire main index synchronously, and a failed overlay should fall back to a valid baseline within the product's freshness contract.

Keep an emergency suppression mechanism outside the slow rebuild cycle. A phrase removed for privacy or safety must be filtered even when some serving replicas still use an older index. Monitor publication progress and retain a rollback manifest; an index that loads successfully can still produce poor or harmful suggestions.
deepDives.invariant: An active index is a complete compatible version, and urgent suppression applies even while an older baseline remains in service.

followUp.question: How can a banned suggestion disappear faster than a daily rebuild?
followUp.answer: Apply a small authoritative suppression overlay at serving time, propagate it with a measured deadline, and remove the phrase from subsequent builds. Do not rely exclusively on rebuilding and warming the full baseline index.

deepDives.title: Privacy, ranking, and cache boundaries
paragraphs: Raw user queries may contain names, addresses, credentials, or private identifiers. Filter sensitive patterns, limit raw retention, and apply support thresholds before allowing query-derived public suggestions. Thresholds reduce exposure but are not a formal anonymity guarantee; private-corpus suggestions require an explicit authorization model.

Personalization changes cache keys and visibility. A shared prefix cache must contain only globally eligible candidates, with user-specific ranking or filtering performed inside the correct boundary. Including one user's private history in a globally cached response leaks data even if the prefix itself is public.

Evaluate suggestions against relevance, coverage, abandonment, and abusive manipulation, not clicks alone. Keep stable evaluation sets by locale, detect coordinated query inflation, and version ranking features. An apparently improved click rate may simply reflect position bias or promotion of already popular phrases.
deepDives.invariant: Private queries or user-specific candidates never enter a public shared suggestion cache merely because their prefixes match.

followUp.question: Can high query frequency alone decide that a phrase is safe to suggest?
followUp.answer: No. Frequency can be manipulated and sensitive phrases can still be common. Use corpus eligibility, privacy filtering, moderation/suppression rules, and relevance evaluation in addition to popularity, with explicit rules for personalized data.

signals.name: Serving budget
signals.measure: Track p99, timeout/fallback rate, candidate counts, and hot prefixes by locale.
signals.response: Bound expansion, cache safe common results, and reduce optional ranking before violating the response deadline.

signals.name: Index freshness
signals.measure: Measure index-version spread, overlay lag, load failures, and rollback availability.
signals.response: Keep the last complete baseline and repair publication rather than serving incompatible partial versions.

signals.name: Suggestion quality
signals.measure: Track empty results, relevance samples, suppression lag, and suspicious query-frequency spikes.
signals.response: Apply urgent suppressions and investigate ranking changes separately from traffic changes.

security: Minimize raw-query logging and remove sensitive material before aggregate phrases become public suggestions.
Keep personalized or authorized-corpus candidates out of shared public caches and bind access checks to serving identity.
Rate-limit query inflation and expensive typo expansion, and audit corpus or suppression-policy changes.
validation: Test Unicode normalization, composition input, empty/long prefixes, and out-of-order client responses using locale-specific cases.
Build a candidate index offline, verify completeness and ranking quality, and canary its versioned publication with rollback.
Inject delayed overlays and suppressed phrases, proving the removal bound even while old index replicas remain active.

prerequisites: Tries, finite-state transducers, and prefix indexes
Top-k ranking, caching, and atomic index publication

functional: Return a small ranked list for a normalized prefix and locale.
Update popularity and freshness from permitted query events.
Filter unsafe or private suggestions and support removal from published results.
nonFunctional: Illustrative target: p99 suggestion responses below 100 ms including the service boundary.
Keep the serving path available while a new index is built.
Set an explicit freshness interval, such as hourly ranking updates with faster emergency suppression.
outOfScope: Full web crawling and ranked document search.
Personalized private-history suggestions in the shared public cache.

assumptions: 100 million searches/day, averaging eight autocomplete requests per search before debouncing and caching.
100 million indexed prefixes with ten 8-byte suggestion IDs per prefix as a simplified upper-level estimate.

estimates.label: Request rate
estimates.calculation: 100,000,000 x 8 / 86,400 = 9,259 requests/s average; 5x peak is about 46,300/s.
estimates.implication: Short prefixes are especially hot. Debounce client requests, cache shared prefix/locale results, and drop stale client responses.

estimates.label: Top-k payload
estimates.calculation: 100,000,000 x 10 x 8 B = 8 GB of suggestion IDs alone.
estimates.implication: Prefix structure, scores, text, locale duplication, and replicas add substantial memory. Avoid claiming the whole index fits in this payload-only estimate.

api.purpose: Normalize Unicode and case consistently, validate length and locale, and bound limit. Return an index version and ranked text/IDs.
Accept eligible anonymized signals with sampling and abuse controls; do not leak raw personal queries into public suggestions.
Add a fast suppression rule and trigger index/cache updates. Restrict this endpoint to authorized moderation operations.

dataModel.notes: Keep display text distinct from normalization. Limit low-frequency terms to reduce accidental exposure of private queries.

flows.name: Serve a prefix
steps: The client debounces typing and tags each request so a slower response for an older prefix cannot overwrite newer suggestions.
The API validates input and applies the same locale-aware normalization used by the index builder.
Look up a shared cache key containing prefix, locale, and index version; otherwise query the appropriate serving shard for bounded top-k candidates.
Apply current suppression rules and return suggestions. Private personalization, if added, must use a separate user-scoped layer.

flows.name: Build and publish
steps: Ingest eligible events, deduplicate, aggregate time-decayed popularity, and remove bot traffic and sensitive or prohibited strings.
Construct new index shards from a consistent input snapshot. Test representative prefixes, language behavior, and memory requirements.
Load and validate the new shards before atomically changing the serving manifest; never expose half an index.
Invalidate or version cache keys, monitor relevance and latency, and roll back the manifest if the new ranking or capacity is worse.

decisions.choice: Precompute a bounded candidate list for popular prefixes.
decisions.tradeOff: This lowers read latency but consumes memory and makes ranking less fresh. On-demand search allows richer filtering but costs more CPU.

decisions.choice: Start with exact prefix completion and add bounded fuzzy matching deliberately.
decisions.tradeOff: Fuzzy expansion can explode candidate work, especially for short strings. Apply minimum lengths, expansion limits, and separate quality measurements.

decisions.choice: Publish versioned batches with a small online overlay for newly trending or suppressed suggestions.
decisions.tradeOff: The overlay improves freshness but complicates ranking and cache invalidation. Keep a clear conflict policy between offline scores and online changes.

failureModes.scenario: An index build fails halfway through.
failureModes.handling: Continue serving the previous complete manifest. Validate checksums and shard availability before publication, and alert on index age.

failureModes.scenario: A short prefix concentrates most requests.
failureModes.handling: Replicate hot-prefix results in local caches and cap fuzzy work. Prefix-based partitioning alone may produce severe skew.

failureModes.scenario: A sensitive query appears as a public suggestion.
failureModes.handling: Apply minimum-frequency and privacy filters, immediate suppression, and cache removal. Track stale response drops, empty-result rate, p99 latency, and moderation propagation time.

selfCheck.question: Why can an autocomplete UI display results for the wrong prefix?
selfCheck.answer: Network responses may arrive out of order. Tag requests with a generation or compare the returned prefix against current input, and ignore older responses; server latency improvements alone do not prevent this client-side race.

selfCheck.question: Why is sharding simply by first character risky?
selfCheck.answer: Traffic and vocabulary are highly uneven across initial characters and languages. Measure shard load, use more flexible partitions, and replicate hot short-prefix results so one shard does not receive most requests.

selfCheck.question: How do you remove a suggestion faster than the next hourly rebuild?
selfCheck.answer: Maintain an authenticated suppression layer checked on the serving path, propagate it promptly, and invalidate matching cache entries. Rebuild the durable index afterward so the removal survives a restart or version change.

design-news-feed.summary: Design a feed of posts from accounts a user follows. Separate durable post ownership from a disposable materialized timeline of post IDs. A hybrid fan-out strategy handles ordinary authors efficiently while avoiding millions of synchronous writes for celebrity accounts; final reads still enforce visibility and deletion rules.
clarifyingQuestions: Is the feed chronological, ranked, or a mixture, and must pagination remain stable during new posts?
What are follower-count and active-reader distributions, including celebrities and returning inactive users?
How do blocks, private follows, deleted posts, reposts, and relationship changes affect eligible history?

deepDives.title: Fan-out as a materialized view
paragraphs: Store the post durably under its author and publish an event through an outbox. Timeline entries are materialized references built later, not the primary post record. This makes fan-out retryable and rebuildable without losing the original content when a worker or cache fails.

Page through eligible followers using durable checkpoints and make each reader/post insertion idempotent. A crash halfway through a fan-out page should repeat safe work, not omit the remaining followers or insert duplicates. Decide whether eligibility is evaluated at publication or read time; final privacy checks are still necessary.

A newly followed author may need bounded history backfill, while an inactive reader may have no materialized inbox at all. Rebuild recent candidates from author streams when required rather than writing every historical post to every dormant account. Keep queue and retention limits explicit so delayed materialization does not become silent permanent loss.
deepDives.invariant: A fan-out retry or rebuild cannot change post ownership or create multiple logical reader/post references in the same timeline.

followUp.question: Why should a post survive even if timeline fan-out fails?
followUp.answer: The timeline is a projection. The durable author-owned post and its event allow workers to retry or rebuild missing references. Making the projection the sole source of truth couples content durability to a large asynchronous fan-out operation.

deepDives.title: Celebrity handling and ranked pagination
paragraphs: Pushing a celebrity post to millions of followers can dominate write capacity, while reading every followed author on demand makes ordinary feed requests expensive. Use hybrid fan-out based on active readership and measured cost, merging high-fan-out author streams at read time with the materialized inbox.

Bound candidate gathering and hydrate posts in batches. Ranking an unlimited history is not compatible with a predictable latency budget. Cache derived candidates where useful, but retain a path to recent authoritative posts when materialization lags. A hot author should not starve the queues of smaller authors.

Chronological cursors can use a cutoff plus a stable timestamp/UUID ordering. Ranked feeds need a rank snapshot, session cursor, or an explicit reordering contract. A mutable score as the only cursor can skip or repeat items between pages; deleting or filtering candidates also requires bounded backfill to avoid empty pages.
deepDives.invariant: Each returned page has deterministic continuation semantics, bounded candidate work, and no duplicate post after hybrid merging.

followUp.question: Can a cursor consisting only of the last ranking score guarantee stable pagination?
followUp.answer: Not when scores change between requests or many posts share a score. Use a stable tie breaker and a snapshot/session rule, or explicitly permit reordering. The pagination contract must match how rankings evolve.

deepDives.title: Read-time eligibility and propagation lag
paragraphs: A user can block an author or lose access to a private account after a timeline reference is written. Filter current visibility during hydration and apply the same rule to direct post endpoints. Removing old inbox entries asynchronously is useful cleanup, not sufficient authorization enforcement.

Use source versions and tombstones for edits and deletes so delayed events cannot resurrect older content. Separate counters and ranking features from authoritative visibility. A stale like count may be acceptable, whereas a stale private-follow grant can expose content to the wrong reader.

Measure freshness as publication-to-eligible-read delay, not merely broker acknowledgment latency. Define degraded behavior when fan-out lags: merge a bounded recent-author window, show a slightly older feed, or disclose temporary unavailability. Do not remove safety filters just to fill a page or hit an engagement metric.
deepDives.invariant: Materialized timeline membership never overrides current authoritative deletion, blocking, or private-account access policy.

followUp.question: Is removing a blocked author's posts from one reader cache enough?
followUp.answer: No. Other caches, profile views, direct links, and late fan-out events can still reference them. Enforce current eligibility at serving boundaries and use cleanup to reclaim stale projections, not as the only privacy mechanism.

signals.name: Fan-out fairness
signals.measure: Track queue age, checkpoint progress, write amplification, and backlog by author cohort.
signals.response: Isolate hot authors, adjust hybrid thresholds, and recover partially applied fan-out idempotently.

signals.name: Read quality
signals.measure: Measure feed p99, candidate hydration cost, duplicate rate, and empty pages after filtering.
signals.response: Bound gathering, batch hydration, and repair cursor or eligibility logic before weakening filters.

signals.name: Visibility freshness
signals.measure: Measure block/delete propagation and attempts to serve stale post versions.
signals.response: Prefer authoritative filtering and stop unsafe projections until their source versions catch up.

security: Authorize private follows and blocks at serving time and derive the reader identity from authentication.
Protect post creation and fan-out endpoints from spam, inflated follower graphs, and tenant-level resource exhaustion.
Minimize retained interaction features, propagate deletion through derived indexes, and audit privileged visibility overrides.
validation: Crash fan-out workers mid-page and replay events; verify no omitted checkpoint range or duplicate timeline reference.
Test celebrity posts, returning inactive users, equal timestamps, rank changes, and pagination under concurrent deletion.
Race follow, block, edit, and delete events; canary new ranking or fan-out policies against privacy and freshness gates, not clicks alone.

Read a paginated feed with recent eligible content.
Honor post deletion, blocks, and audience changes even when timeline entries are stale.

Allow bounded feed freshness lag after publication; do not relax access checks.

estimates.calculation: 20,000,000 x 500 x 16 B = 160 GB raw timeline references.
estimates.implication: Cache IDs rather than full post bodies; object overhead, scores, and replicas increase actual memory. Inactive users may be reconstructed on demand.

api.purpose: Persist a post and outbox event idempotently, then acknowledge without waiting for all follower timelines.
Return hydrated eligible posts and a stable next cursor. Bound page size and deduplicate candidates.
Change the graph idempotently and trigger bounded backfill or cleanup as needed. Enforce the current relationship during reads.

flows.name: Publish a post
steps: Persist the post and outbox event in one transaction, then acknowledge the author.
For ordinary authors, paginate eligible followers and enqueue bounded fan-out batches.
Workers insert post IDs idempotently into active users' timelines and trim to retention limits.
For high-fanout authors, retain recent posts in an author stream for read-time merging instead of pushing to every follower.

flows.name: Assemble a feed
steps: Load the viewer's materialized timeline and recent posts from followed high-fanout authors.
Merge and deduplicate candidates with a stable sort key or a snapshot ranking context.
Batch-hydrate posts and enforce current deletion, block, and audience rules. Fetch extra candidates if filtering empties the page.
Return an opaque cursor tied to the ordering policy. A changing ranking score needs snapshot or session semantics to reduce repeats and skipped items.

decisions.choice: Push ordinary authors and pull very high-fanout authors during reads.
decisions.tradeOff: There is no universal follower-count threshold. Choose it using posting rate, follower activity, read frequency, and measured read/insert costs.

decisions.choice: Materialize IDs and scores, then batch-hydrate post bodies.
decisions.tradeOff: This avoids copying large bodies and simplifies edits, but adds a hydration dependency that needs caching and bounded partial-failure behavior.

decisions.choice: Allow asynchronous timeline updates while treating privacy checks as authoritative at read time.
decisions.tradeOff: A stale feed can omit a recent post, but it must not expose a now-private one. These are different consistency requirements.

failureModes.scenario: A celebrity post produces millions of fan-out tasks.
failureModes.handling: Route high-fanout authors to the pull path, batch work, and apply per-author fairness so ordinary posts continue to propagate.

failureModes.scenario: Fan-out events are replayed after a worker crash.
failureModes.handling: Use unique viewer/post keys or set-like insertion. Replays must not show duplicate posts or consume all timeline slots.

failureModes.scenario: A deleted post remains in cached timelines.
failureModes.handling: Filter against authoritative post state and propagate tombstones. Monitor fan-out lag, feed p99, hydration failures, cache misses, and visibility-filter rejects.

selfCheck.question: Why is fan-out on write expensive for a celebrity?
selfCheck.answer: Each post creates work proportional to the eligible follower count, including many inactive users who may never read it. A pull or hybrid path shifts that work to actual feed reads, at the cost of more read-time merging and caching.

selfCheck.question: Can a cached timeline be trusted to enforce post privacy?
selfCheck.answer: No. Audience changes, blocks, unfollows, and deletion can happen after fan-out. Revalidate visibility during hydration or use a comparably strong access-control mechanism; asynchronous cleanup alone creates a data-exposure window.

selfCheck.question: Why is offset pagination unstable for a changing feed?
selfCheck.answer: New inserts and ranking changes shift row positions, causing repeated or skipped posts between pages. Use an opaque cursor with stable tie-breakers and, for changing rankings, a snapshot or session context with explicit freshness behavior.

design-recommendation-system.summary: Design a recommendation pipeline using video discovery as a concrete example. Separate candidate retrieval, ranking, and re-ranking so expensive models see a manageable candidate set. The system must optimize a stated user outcome, prevent training-data leakage, serve within a latency budget, and remain useful when models or features are unavailable.
clarifyingQuestions: What user outcome is being optimized, and which quality, diversity, or safety constraints must not regress?
How fresh must interactions and catalog features be, and what latency budget is available for retrieval and ranking?
How do new users/items, opt-outs, regional eligibility, and model outages behave?

deepDives.title: Candidate retrieval and bounded ranking
paragraphs: Separate retrieving a few hundred plausible items from scoring them with an expensive model. Candidate sources can include subscriptions, recent popularity, collaborative signals, and an approximate nearest-neighbor index. Measure each source's recall and coverage; ranking cannot recover a relevant item that retrieval never included.

Allocate an end-to-end latency budget across feature lookup, retrieval, scoring, and final filtering. Fetch features in batches and cap candidate counts. Parallelism is useful only with bounded work and cancellation; an unavailable feature service must not turn each request into hundreds of individually timed-out calls.

Enforce hard eligibility after candidate assembly and on every fallback: deleted titles, blocked creators, regional rights, and account restrictions cannot be overridden by a high relevance score. Keep model, feature schema, and item-index versions compatible so a successful request does not silently score the wrong feature representation.
deepDives.invariant: No model score or fallback can bypass current item eligibility, and ranking operates on a bounded compatible candidate/feature set.

followUp.question: Why can a better ranking model fail to improve recommendations?
followUp.answer: The candidate stage may never retrieve the useful items, or eligibility filters may remove them. Evaluate retrieval recall, coverage, feature freshness, and final result composition independently before attributing all quality to the ranker.

deepDives.title: Point-in-time data and feedback bias
paragraphs: Training rows must use features that existed at the decision time, not values updated after the outcome. Otherwise future clicks, purchases, or popularity leak into training and make offline performance misleading. Join features by event time and retain the provenance needed to reproduce the training snapshot.

Log impressions and the served model/version, not only positive interactions. An unclicked unseen item is not the same as an exposed negative example, and position affects response probability. Define labels, attribution windows, and delayed outcomes carefully before choosing sampling or loss functions.

Recommendation changes influence the next round of collected data. Purely exploiting current popularity can narrow coverage and amplify historical exposure. Evaluate controlled exploration, diversity, and user-quality guardrails with appropriately randomized experiments rather than interpreting a short-term click lift as universally better recommendations.
deepDives.invariant: Offline training and evaluation cannot use future information or pretend an item was exposed when the user never had a chance to interact with it.

followUp.question: What is a point-in-time correct feature join?
followUp.answer: It selects the latest feature version available at or before the recommendation decision, respecting processing availability where relevant. Joining today's aggregate to an old training example can leak the outcome or future behavior and inflate offline scores.

deepDives.title: Cold starts, fallbacks, and model rollout
paragraphs: New users and new items lack historical interactions. Use explicit onboarding preferences, content features, and appropriately scoped popularity without fabricating confidence. A cold-start policy should preserve eligibility and provide diverse useful candidates while gradually incorporating real behavior.

Retain a simple fallback list or previous compatible model for service outages. Define which optional features may default and which missing features require fallback. A stale feature can be more dangerous than an absent one if the model interprets it as current; include freshness in the feature contract.

Shadow and canary new model bundles with a compatible retrieval index and feature schema. Track latency, fallback use, business quality, and user guardrails by cohort. Keep rollback artifacts and inference reproducibility; replacing weights alone may not restore behavior after a simultaneous incompatible feature-pipeline change.
deepDives.invariant: A model rollout or outage fallback remains eligible, bounded, and compatible with the feature/index versions used to produce its results.

followUp.question: Why is storing only the model weights insufficient for rollback?
followUp.answer: Predictions also depend on feature transformations, schema, retrieval index, and serving code. Version the complete compatible bundle and retain the prior feature path or migration strategy so rollback can reproduce the previous behavior.

signals.name: Serving budget
signals.measure: Measure retrieval/ranking latency, feature timeout rate, candidate count, and fallback rate by model version.
signals.response: Disable optional expensive stages and revert to a compatible eligible fallback before deadlines cascade.

signals.name: Data and model quality
signals.measure: Track feature freshness, null distributions, retrieval recall, exposure mix, and label delay.
signals.response: Repair data pipelines or candidate coverage before repeatedly retraining on biased or incomplete inputs.

signals.name: Experiment guardrails
signals.measure: Measure user-quality outcomes, diversity, eligibility violations, and latency by randomized cohort.
signals.response: Stop a harmful or incompatible experiment and retain versioned evidence for diagnosis.

security: Honor interaction opt-outs and access restrictions; pseudonymous identifiers are still sensitive and need retention controls.
Apply item safety and regional eligibility to every retrieval source and fallback, not just the main ranker.
Restrict feature/model publication and training-data access, audit provenance, and document the limits of deleting information already learned by a model.
validation: Replay historical decisions with point-in-time features and test for future leakage and missing-impression bias.
Inject unavailable or stale feature services and incompatible bundle versions; verify bounded eligible fallbacks.
Run staged experiments with sticky randomized cohorts, predefined guardrails, and rollback of the entire serving bundle.

Record impressions and subsequent engagement with attribution IDs.
Train, evaluate, deploy, and roll back versioned recommendation models.
nonFunctional: Illustrative target: p99 recommendation responses below 200 ms for the online service.
Enforce content eligibility, user controls, and privacy rules independently of model scores.
Maintain a useful fallback for new users, sparse data, or serving outages.

assumptions: 100 million daily active users request 20 recommendation lists/day.
Each request ranks 500 retrieved candidates; an item index holds 100 million 256-dimensional float32 embeddings.

estimates.label: Online ranking load
estimates.calculation: 2,000,000,000 / 86,400 = 23,148 requests/s; x 500 candidates = 11.57 million candidate scores/s average.
estimates.implication: Use cheap candidate generation, batching, model optimization, and a staged latency budget. Measure peak load and hardware-specific inference throughput.

estimates.label: Embedding payload
estimates.calculation: 100,000,000 x 256 x 4 B = 102.4 GB raw vectors.
estimates.implication: ANN graph/index overhead and replicas add memory. Quantization and sharding trade accuracy, latency, and operational complexity.

flowchart TD

 Retrieval --> Ranker[Ranking model]

flows.name: Recommend online
steps: Fetch user context and run several bounded retrieval sources, such as embeddings, subscriptions, and fresh/popular items.
Deduplicate candidates, exclude ineligible items early, and batch-fetch version-compatible features.
Score candidates within the remaining deadline, then apply safety, diversity, repetition, and business constraints in a separate re-ranking stage.
Return the selected list with attribution IDs. Fall back to safe cached or popularity-based results if a critical online dependency is unavailable.

flows.name: Train and improve
steps: Collect impressions and delayed outcomes, respecting consent and deletion rules; distinguish event time from ingestion time.
Build labels and point-in-time features, split evaluation data chronologically, and check for popularity and position biases.
Compare against simple baselines using offline ranking metrics and product guardrails, then run a controlled online experiment.
Deploy versioned bundles gradually. Monitor engagement quality, latency, diversity, feature drift, and feedback loops before expanding traffic.

decisions.choice: Choose a measurable user outcome such as satisfying watch time or long-term engagement, with quality and safety guardrails.
decisions.tradeOff: Maximizing clicks alone can reward clickbait; watch time alone can favor long content. A model metric is not automatically a product objective.

decisions.choice: Use cheap retrieval to reduce millions of items to hundreds before expensive ranking.
decisions.tradeOff: The ranker cannot recover relevant items retrieval omitted. Evaluate retrieval recall separately from ranking quality.

decisions.choice: Blend batch features with fresh interaction signals and a content/popularity fallback.
decisions.tradeOff: Fresh signals improve adaptation but increase serving dependencies and feedback-loop risk. New users and items need explicit exploration policies.

failureModes.scenario: The online feature store is slow or missing values.
failureModes.handling: Use bounded timeouts and trained default/missing-value behavior, then a safe fallback. Randomly substituting values can invalidate model calibration.

failureModes.scenario: A new model improves offline accuracy but harms users.
failureModes.handling: Use canary experiments, guardrails, and rollback; investigate data leakage, exposure bias, latency, and objective mismatch.

failureModes.scenario: Training and serving use incompatible feature definitions.
failureModes.handling: Version schemas and transformations, validate bundle compatibility, and monitor missing-feature rate, drift, serving latency, coverage, and diversity.

selfCheck.question: Why log impressions rather than only clicks?
selfCheck.answer: Without knowing what a user was shown, the system cannot distinguish ignored items from items never exposed. Impression IDs also connect delayed outcomes to the recommendation and model version that produced them, enabling more defensible evaluation.

selfCheck.question: What is point-in-time leakage?
selfCheck.answer: It occurs when a training example uses information that was unavailable at the moment of prediction, such as a later popularity total. Offline performance becomes unrealistically strong; time-aware joins and chronological validation help detect and prevent it.

selfCheck.question: Can a better ranker fix poor candidate retrieval?
selfCheck.answer: Only within the candidates it receives. If relevant items never enter the candidate set, no downstream score can select them. Measure retrieval recall, mix complementary sources, and evaluate the entire pipeline rather than one model in isolation.

design-analytics-event-pipeline.summary: Design an event ingestion and aggregation pipeline using ad-click analytics as the worked example. Keep a durable raw log so aggregates can be rebuilt. Define event-time windows, late-arrival rules, deduplication scope, and sink semantics before promising accurate counts; fast ingestion alone does not make the resulting dashboard correct.
clarifyingQuestions: Are aggregates approximate dashboards or financial/accounting inputs requiring exact reconciliation?
What are the allowed duplicate and late-arrival windows, and how much clock skew is tolerated?
How long is raw history retained, and must historical backfills coexist with live processing?

deepDives.title: Durable ingestion and deduplication scope
paragraphs: Validate identity, schema, size, and event-time bounds before acknowledging accepted events. Give logical events stable UUIDs so a producer retry does not become a new event. Persist accepted raw data durably before responding when loss is outside the product contract, and distinguish rejected records from temporarily unavailable ingestion.

Deduplication has a scope and retention cost. At 500,000 events/s, one day contains 43.2 billion event IDs; even 16 bytes each is 691.2 GB before indexing. Choose the required duplicate window and partitioning deliberately instead of proposing an unlimited in-memory set.

Probabilistic structures can help prefilter lookup but may introduce false positives. That can be acceptable for an explicitly approximate dashboard, not automatically for billable click accounting. Keep raw evidence and a reconciliation route so analytical approximations do not silently become financial truth.
deepDives.invariant: The pipeline's accepted-event durability and duplicate window are explicit, and approximate deduplication is not represented as exact accounting.

followUp.question: Is an event UUID enough to guarantee deduplication forever?
followUp.answer: No. It provides an identity to compare, but the processor must retain or otherwise recover the set of processed identities for the promised window. Storage, partitioning, retention, and replay semantics determine the actual guarantee.

deepDives.title: Event-time windows and correct checkpoints
paragraphs: Processing time describes arrival at your service; event time describes when the interaction occurred. Define window boundaries, allowed lateness, and watermark behavior so delayed mobile or offline events do not disappear unpredictably. Validate extreme timestamps without assuming every producer clock is trustworthy.

Checkpoint input position together with aggregate state through a supported transactional or versioned sink protocol. Writing an aggregate and later committing an offset can double-count after a crash; committing first can lose the effect. An idempotent upsert of a versioned window result can be safer than blindly incrementing the sink on every replay.

Late events may update an open window, create a correction, or be retained only for offline recomputation according to contract. Keep revisions distinguishable and make downstream consumers handle them idempotently. A dashboard showing the latest corrected result and an immutable accounting statement may require different publication policies.
deepDives.invariant: A recovered checkpoint corresponds to the aggregate state it claims, and late-event revisions are not applied twice as fresh independent increments.

followUp.question: What does a watermark actually guarantee?
followUp.answer: It is an estimate or policy boundary for event-time progress, not proof that no older event can ever arrive. Define how late arrivals beyond it are handled and whether published windows can be corrected or reconciled later.

deepDives.title: Hot keys and isolated backfills
paragraphs: One popular advertisement or tenant can dominate a partition even with balanced event IDs elsewhere. Use a two-stage aggregation with a stable salt or subpartition when the aggregation is mergeable, then combine partials. For distinct counts or non-associative logic, explain the accuracy and state implications rather than assuming arbitrary splitting is safe.

Backfills should read immutable raw history and write to an isolated computation version or output namespace. Verify results and switch consumers deliberately instead of adding replayed counts into the live output. Keep event schema and transformation versions so historical input can be interpreted reproducibly.

Limit backfill IO and compute to preserve the live pipeline's recovery margin. Monitor lag by time and bytes, not only record count, and retain enough raw history to recover. Poison records need a durable quarantine path with reasons and replay ownership; repeatedly retrying one malformed event can block useful ordered work.
deepDives.invariant: Historical replay cannot mix with live aggregation in a way that counts the same input twice or silently changes the computation definition.

followUp.question: How can you recompute last month's aggregates without inflating today's totals?
followUp.answer: Read the retained raw history into a separate versioned output, validate it, then replace or reconcile the intended historical windows. Do not send a backfill through a live increment-only sink without explicit replay and version semantics.

signals.name: Ingestion and lag
signals.measure: Track acknowledged durable events, rejects, event-time skew, and consumer lag in time and bytes.
signals.response: Protect ingestion capacity, quarantine invalid records, and restore processing before retained history expires.

signals.name: Counting correctness
signals.measure: Measure duplicate rate, late corrections, checkpoint recovery, and raw-to-aggregate reconciliation differences.
signals.response: Stop publishing incorrect revisions and replay into an isolated output version for repair.

signals.name: Skew and replay cost
signals.measure: Track hot-key state, per-partition throughput, deduplication memory, and backfill resource share.
signals.response: Apply merge-safe partial aggregation and constrain historical work to preserve live recovery headroom.

security: Authenticate event producers and bind tenant attribution to trusted credentials rather than editable event fields.
Minimize raw identifiers and sensitive URLs, encrypt retained data, and enforce deletion across archives and derived datasets.
Restrict schema and computation publication; isolate malformed payloads and oversized or highly compressed records before expensive processing.
validation: Inject duplicates, out-of-order events, clock skew, and crashes between state writes and offset commits; reconcile against a small exact oracle.
Replay historical schemas into a new computation version and verify corrections cannot double-count in downstream consumers.
Load-test a hot key and a concurrent backfill, then canary new window/retention policies with rollback and raw-data recovery evidence.

functional: Ingest validated events with stable IDs and schema versions.
Aggregate counts and dimensions over defined time windows.

nonFunctional: Illustrative target: ordinary events appear in provisional aggregates within one minute.
Do not lose acknowledged ingestion within the agreed log durability model.

outOfScope: Billing-grade final financial settlement from untrusted client click events.

Keep one day of event IDs for deduplication only if required; a 16-byte ID is a payload lower bound.

estimates.label: Ingestion and retention
estimates.implication: Partition ingestion, compress batches, and archive to object storage with lifecycle rules. Replication multiplies hot-log capacity.

estimates.label: Deduplication state
estimates.calculation: 500,000 x 86,400 x 16 B = 691.2 GB of IDs for one day, excluding state-store overhead.
estimates.implication: Deduplication is not free. Choose a justified retention horizon, partition state, and define what happens to duplicates outside that horizon.

api.purpose: Validate sizes, identity, event IDs, and timestamp bounds; acknowledge only after durable append and return per-event validation results where needed.
Read bounded aggregate ranges and expose freshness/finalization metadata, not just a count with no time semantics.
Run a controlled backfill into a separate output version before replacing live aggregates.

flows.name: Ingest and aggregate
steps: Validate schema and payload, assign an ingest timestamp, and preserve a caller-stable event ID across retries.
Append to a replicated log, acknowledge at the configured durability boundary, and archive immutable raw events asynchronously.
Partition processing by aggregation key, deduplicate within the declared horizon, and assign windows using event time.
Advance watermarks according to the observed delay policy and write provisional/revised aggregates with replay-safe sink semantics.

flows.name: Handle late data and backfills
steps: Route events behind the watermark according to allowed lateness: update a revision, send to a correction stream, or reject with an explicit policy.
Checkpoint source positions and processing state consistently so a restart does not combine new offsets with old counts.
Replay archived data into a versioned output namespace using the intended schema and pipeline version.
Compare totals and sample records before atomically switching query consumers to the corrected output; throttle backfills so live traffic remains healthy.

decisions.choice: Use event time for business windows and watermarks to bound how long to wait.
decisions.tradeOff: A watermark is a progress assumption, not proof that no earlier event exists. Faster finalization trades off against late corrections.

decisions.choice: Use partial aggregates on salted subkeys and a second-stage merge for associative operations.
decisions.tradeOff: This reduces skew but complicates deduplication and corrections. Non-associative metrics need a different merge strategy.

decisions.choice: Bind checkpoint recovery to transactional or idempotent output writes.
decisions.tradeOff: Exactly-once processing inside a stream engine does not automatically make an external increment API exactly once.

failureModes.scenario: A producer retries an entire batch after an ambiguous response.
failureModes.handling: Retain stable event IDs and deduplicate within the supported horizon. Random IDs on every retry defeat deduplication.

failureModes.scenario: One partition is idle and prevents watermark progress.
failureModes.handling: Use deliberate idle-partition detection and lateness rules, while handling resumed old events as late data. Monitor event-time lag separately from CPU usage.

failureModes.scenario: A schema change breaks consumers or a replay overwrites live data.
failureModes.handling: Check compatibility, quarantine poison records, version pipeline outputs, and isolate replays. Monitor checkpoint duration, sink lag, duplicate rate, late-event volume, and reconciliation differences.

selfCheck.question: What does a watermark actually mean?
selfCheck.answer: It expresses a processing system's assumption about how far event time has progressed, based on a lateness policy. It is not a guarantee that all earlier events have arrived; define allowed lateness and how corrections affect already published aggregates.

selfCheck.question: Why can replaying raw events double dashboard counts?
selfCheck.answer: If the sink applies another increment for each replayed record, it repeats effects already committed before the failure or backfill. Use transactional checkpoints, idempotent event effects, or replace versioned window aggregates instead of blindly adding again.

selfCheck.question: How do you keep a multi-day backfill from delaying current analytics?
selfCheck.answer: Separate replay compute and output versions, cap its source and sink bandwidth, and prioritize live processing. Validate the rebuilt dataset before switching readers; otherwise a backfill can both overload production and expose partially recomputed totals.

design-ride-sharing-platform.summary: Design trip requests, nearby-driver search, and assignment for a ride-sharing service. Location updates are frequent and may be stale; trip ownership must be authoritative. Use the geospatial index to find candidates, then reserve a driver through a concurrency-safe dispatch state machine rather than assuming the nearest indexed driver is still free.
clarifyingQuestions: Are we matching one rider to one driver, or supporting pools, scheduled rides, and multiple vehicle classes?
How stale may driver locations be, and what counts as an online available driver?
What are the acceptance, cancellation, pricing, and regional ownership rules during dispatch and failover?

deepDives.title: Geospatial candidates are not availability
paragraphs: Use a spatial index to find a bounded set of nearby drivers, then consult authoritative availability before offering or assigning. Location messages can be delayed, reordered, or missing. Keep per-driver update sequence and freshness metadata so an old GPS message cannot make an offline or distant driver appear newly available.

Search neighboring cells and expand the radius when appropriate; the nearest driver may lie just across a grid boundary. Geographic distance is a broad-phase filter, not the final pickup estimate. Apply vehicle eligibility and a bounded road-network ETA computation only to promising candidates.

Hot downtown cells need different handling from quiet regions. Partition location ingestion and cache candidate lists carefully, but retain a separate driver assignment authority. More frequent GPS updates improve freshness at significant write and battery cost; adaptive reporting and age-aware ranking are product trade-offs, not substitutes for ownership checks.
deepDives.invariant: A stale geospatial index can nominate a candidate but cannot declare that driver unconditionally available or assign them without an authoritative transition.

followUp.question: Why can the nearest indexed driver be the wrong choice?
followUp.answer: The position may be stale, the driver may already be assigned, or road topology may make pickup slower than a geographically farther candidate. Use the index for bounded discovery, then validate availability and estimate route-aware pickup cost.

deepDives.title: Offer leases and one-driver-one-trip ownership
paragraphs: Represent trip requests, offers, and accepted assignments as durable states with UUIDs. A driver accepting an offer must match its current lease identity and version; a late acceptance after expiry must not revive an old dispatch attempt. Client retries reuse request identity instead of creating another trip.

Within a dispatch ownership domain, use a transaction or equivalent conditional protocol enforcing both one active assignment per driver and one accepted driver per trip. If driver and trip authorities are separated, explicitly reserve, confirm, fence, and recover the cross-owner transition. Two independent unconditional updates do not make a correct assignment.

Race cancellation against acceptance at the same authoritative boundary and define which transition wins. Publish assignment and cancellation effects through an outbox so rider and driver notifications can retry. A missing notification changes what a participant sees, not who actually owns the trip.
deepDives.invariant: At most one active trip owns a driver and at most one accepted driver owns a trip; expired offer generations cannot acquire either ownership.

followUp.question: Is a compare-and-set on driver availability enough to complete dispatch?
followUp.answer: It protects that driver's claim, but the trip must also prevent multiple accepted drivers and handle cancellation. Enforce both sides in one ownership boundary or a fenced recoverable protocol, with idempotent compensation for incomplete reservations.

deepDives.title: Regional handoff and user-visible recovery
paragraphs: Regionalize high-frequency location and dispatch work near a city or service area. Moving a driver between ownership domains requires a versioned handoff that fences the old owner. Letting both regions independently accept offers during a partition can violate assignment guarantees even if their location indexes eventually converge.

Treat rider and driver connectivity as intermittent. Reconnecting clients fetch authoritative trip state and replay missed events through a cursor or version, rather than guessing from their last screen. A lost GPS stream should be shown as stale, not rendered as verified current movement.

Keep fare quote versions, trip lifecycle, and payment attempts separate. A revised ETA or route does not automatically authorize a new charge. Handle canceled pickups, no-shows, and completed rides through explicit policy transitions and reconciliation, with an audit trail usable when the participants' reported outcomes disagree.
deepDives.invariant: Ownership handoff and reconnection preserve the same authoritative trip identity and do not treat stale location or UI state as proof of a lifecycle transition.

followUp.question: What should happen when a driver reconnects after dispatch failed over?
followUp.answer: Authenticate the device, load the current driver/trip generation from the authority, reject obsolete offer actions, and replay relevant state. Do not infer availability from an old local 'idle' flag or silently create a replacement trip.

signals.name: Matching quality
signals.measure: Track request-to-offer/accept latency, candidate freshness, no-driver rate, and pickup ETA error by geography.
signals.response: Separate true supply shortage from stale indexes or dispatch failures before expanding search or increasing offers.

signals.name: Assignment correctness
signals.measure: Alert on conflicting active assignments, stale-lease acceptance, and cancellation/acceptance anomalies.
signals.response: Fence affected ownership domains and reconcile participants before issuing new offers.

signals.name: Location and connectivity
signals.measure: Measure update age, dropped/reordered positions, reconnect rates, and cell hotspots.
signals.response: Apply freshness filtering, adaptive ingestion, and bounded regional recovery without inventing live positions.

security: Authorize rider and driver operations against the current trip and device identity, not just a supplied trip UUID.
Minimize precise-location retention and visibility, restrict operator access, and audit access to historical routes.
Validate impossible location changes and abuse signals while keeping assignment correctness independent of untrusted client availability claims.
validation: Race multiple riders and offers for the same driver, including cancellation, lease expiry, retries, and delayed acceptance.
Replay out-of-order location updates near spatial boundaries and compare bounded candidate search with known route-aware cases.
Rehearse regional ownership handoff and device reconnects, then canary dispatch policies with assignment and pickup-quality rollback gates.

Track available drivers, find eligible nearby candidates, and offer a trip.
Manage acceptance, arrival, pickup, completion, cancellation, and live trip location.
nonFunctional: Illustrative target: nearby-driver lookup below 200 ms; assignment completes within a bounded offer window.
Never assign a driver to conflicting active trips in the authoritative state.
Tolerate stale GPS, reconnects, and a failed dispatch worker without losing trip ownership.
outOfScope: A full routing engine, surge-pricing model, and payment processor.
A single globally ordered location log across all cities.

assumptions: 2 million online drivers report location every four seconds.

estimates.label: Location traffic
estimates.calculation: 2,000,000 / 4 = 500,000 location updates/s.
estimates.implication: Partition geographically and keep latest positions in a fast expiring index. Persist sampled/history events separately from transaction-heavy trip state.

estimates.label: Matching traffic
estimates.calculation: 10,000,000 / 86,400 = 116 requests/s average; at 5x peak, 579/s x 200 = about 116,000 candidate checks/s.
estimates.implication: GPS ingestion and assignment have very different throughput and consistency needs. Do not send every GPS update through the trip transaction database.

api.purpose: Authenticate the driver, reject older updates, validate coordinates, and refresh availability-location TTL.
Create an idempotent trip request tied to an expiring quote; return a stable trip ID and initial state.
Atomically verify an unexpired offer and reserve both the trip and driver. Reject stale or conflicting acceptance.

dataModel.notes: Use validated, idempotent transitions with a version check. The trip database owns assignment, not the GPS index.

flows.name: Find and reserve a driver
steps: Create a trip idempotently, select the pickup region, and query nearby cells for candidates with fresh location timestamps.
Expand neighboring cells as needed, then refine by distance, route ETA, vehicle eligibility, and driver state. A cell match is only a coarse filter.
Create a bounded offer/reservation through an atomic state transition with an expiry and fencing version.
Accept only the current offer and transition the trip/driver together. Expired, duplicate, or late acceptances return the authoritative outcome.

flows.name: Run the trip
steps: Persist validated state transitions such as assigned, arrived, in_progress, and completed with a state version.
Deliver live location through a transient channel while retaining authoritative trip state independently.
On reconnect, read current trip state and resume events from a cursor; do not reconstruct ownership from mobile-client memory.
On completion or cancellation, release the driver in the authority and publish an outbox event for downstream billing and notifications.

decisions.choice: Partition location and dispatch primarily by city or region, with cell-based candidate lookup.
decisions.tradeOff: Borders and dense hotspots need overlap queries and load-aware partitioning. A geographic cell ID is not a road-distance measurement.

decisions.choice: Start with a short sequential offer or tightly controlled reservation window.
decisions.tradeOff: Broadcast offers reduce matching latency but create more contention and disappointed late acceptances; the authoritative reservation must still be singular.

decisions.choice: Allow approximate locations while making assignment transitions strongly coordinated within their ownership boundary.
decisions.tradeOff: Treating every GPS update as strongly consistent is costly; treating assignment as eventually consistent can double-book a driver.

failureModes.scenario: Two workers select the same driver.
failureModes.handling: Both may see the same index entry, but only one conditional reservation should succeed. Retry matching after an authoritative conflict.

failureModes.scenario: An old offer is accepted after its lease expired.
failureModes.handling: Check expiry and fencing version in the authoritative transaction, not just on the device. Never revive an obsolete lease.

failureModes.scenario: A city becomes a location-update hotspot.
failureModes.handling: Split or replicate read indexes, throttle stale updates, and isolate regional queues. Monitor location age, match latency, lease conflicts, offer expiry, and trip-state divergence.

selfCheck.question: Why is a geospatial cache insufficient to prevent double booking?
selfCheck.answer: Multiple workers can read the same available-driver snapshot, and GPS/index updates may be delayed. A concurrency-safe reservation in an authoritative store must decide ownership; the spatial index only helps generate candidates.

selfCheck.question: What does a fencing version add beyond an expiry timestamp?
selfCheck.answer: It identifies the current ownership generation, so a delayed worker or client cannot act on an old lease after a new one has been issued. The receiving authority must reject older versions for fencing to provide protection.

selfCheck.question: Can the nearest driver by straight-line distance always be the best match?
selfCheck.answer: No. Road layout, traffic, bridges, direction, vehicle type, and pickup access can make another driver faster or eligible. Use cells and straight-line distance for candidate generation, then refine using routing and product constraints.
