design-food-delivery-platform.summary: Design a local food-delivery workflow connecting customers, merchants, couriers, and payment providers. A restaurant marketplace differs from a warehouse-based service such as Gopuff, especially around merchant acceptance and inventory. Model the order as a durable state machine with explicit compensations rather than pretending all participants share one transaction.
clarifyingQuestions: Do merchants accept and prepare orders, or does the platform own warehouse inventory like a quick-commerce service?
When are payment, preparation, courier assignment, pickup, and cancellation financially committed?
Do we support one order per courier or batching, and how much ETA uncertainty is acceptable?

deepDives.title: An order saga with irreversible steps
paragraphs: A food order coordinates the customer, merchant, courier, and payment provider, none of which share one database transaction. Persist the workflow and each participant command identity. A merchant timeout may mean the kitchen accepted the order but the response was lost; retrying with a new identity can produce duplicate preparation.

Model accepted, preparing, ready, picked-up, delivered, canceled, and compensation-pending states with legal transitions. Cooking and pickup are not reversible database writes. Compensation may mean a refund, merchant reimbursement, or support workflow rather than restoring the world to its pre-order state.

Publish transitions through an outbox and process participant events idempotently with versions. If a late 'accepted' event arrives after a cancellation decision, resolve it according to policy instead of blindly rewinding the order. Track unresolved compensation as durable work until its external outcome is verified.
deepDives.invariant: One order identity owns its participant commands, and cancellation cannot pretend an irreversible preparation or pickup step never happened.

followUp.question: Why is a saga not simply a database rollback across services?
followUp.answer: Its participants may already have performed irreversible real-world work. A saga records progress and compensating business actions, which can themselves fail or require human resolution. It does not make preparation, pickup, or external payments atomically reversible.

deepDives.title: Preparation-aware dispatch and ETA
paragraphs: Matching the geographically nearest courier immediately can make them wait at a kitchen that is not ready. Combine merchant preparation estimates, courier pickup travel, and current workflow state. Keep preparation and route estimates separately measurable rather than hiding both errors in one opaque delivery ETA.

Use a spatial candidate index for discovery and an authoritative lease for courier assignment, just as in ride dispatch. Revalidate availability and order eligibility before confirming. If batching is added, capacity, pickup precedence, food freshness, and promised deadlines become constraints on the route, not simply another nearest-neighbor lookup.

Location and merchant readiness messages can be stale or optimistic. Preserve event timestamps and versions, expose uncertainty, and escalate stalled orders. A missed courier heartbeat should trigger an investigation or safe reassignment protocol rather than immediately assigning the same picked-up parcel to another courier.
deepDives.invariant: A courier assignment is confirmed only against current order and courier ownership; stale readiness or GPS data cannot duplicate physical delivery responsibility.

followUp.question: Why might the nearest courier increase delivery time?
followUp.answer: They may arrive long before preparation finishes, displacing a better-timed assignment or missing another delivery commitment. Optimize the combined preparation and travel timeline under capacity and freshness constraints, not straight-line distance alone.

deepDives.title: Menu projections, pricing, and reconciliation
paragraphs: Menus and availability are read projections, while the merchant must accept the actual requested items and price terms. Snapshot item options, taxes, fees, discounts, and quoted totals on the order. A later menu edit cannot silently alter what the customer agreed to buy.

Separate payment authorization/capture, customer refund, merchant settlement, and courier payout. They represent different financial obligations and may settle at different times. Use durable attempt identities and a ledger/reconciliation boundary rather than treating the order's displayed 'delivered' label as a complete accounting system.

A restaurant marketplace has merchant acceptance and preparation uncertainty; a warehouse model instead owns stock allocation and picking capacity. Reuse the durable workflow pattern but do not substitute one domain's inventory assumptions for the other. State which participant is authoritative for each item, time estimate, and financial outcome.
deepDives.invariant: Order terms and financial obligations are not rewritten by a stale menu projection or by an unrelated delivery-status update.

followUp.question: Can a warehouse-delivery design be reused unchanged for restaurant delivery?
followUp.answer: No. A restaurant may reject items, change preparation time, or begin irreversible cooking after acceptance. The platform needs merchant coordination and compensation policies that differ from directly reserving and picking its own inventory.

signals.name: Workflow age
signals.measure: Track time spent awaiting merchant, preparing, waiting for courier, and compensation pending.
signals.response: Escalate the specific stalled participant and recover by command identity rather than restarting the entire order.

signals.name: ETA and assignment
signals.measure: Measure preparation error, pickup wait, delivery lateness, lease conflicts, and location freshness.
signals.response: Adjust dispatch timing or capacity while preserving ownership of already-picked-up orders.

signals.name: Financial consistency
signals.measure: Track unknown payments, refund age, settlement discrepancies, and duplicate merchant commands.
signals.response: Reconcile participant outcomes and hold unsafe payouts or captures until the obligation is understood.

security: Authorize merchant, courier, and customer actions by order role; verify signed partner callbacks and ignore client-supplied final prices.
Minimize address and precise-location exposure to only the participants and time windows that need it.
Protect coupons, refunds, and administrative overrides with rate limits, auditable policy, and scoped operator permissions.
validation: Inject lost merchant acknowledgments, delayed readiness, payment timeouts, and duplicate participant events at each workflow stage.
Race cancellation with preparation, pickup, and courier reassignment; verify compensation policy without impossible state rewinds.
Simulate meal-time hotspots and bad ETA predictions, then canary dispatch changes with preparation, delivery, and financial guardrails.

Geospatial dispatch, payment authorization, and expiring reservations

functional: Browse nearby merchants and create an order from a price/menu snapshot.
Coordinate payment authorization, merchant acceptance, courier assignment, and delivery.
Track order status and handle rejection, cancellation, refund, and support intervention.
nonFunctional: Illustrative target: order submission below one second excluding external confirmation; later steps may be asynchronous.
Avoid duplicate charges, conflicting courier assignments, and invalid order transitions.
Keep an auditable recovery path when a merchant, courier, or payment provider is unavailable.
outOfScope: A complete route-optimization engine and dynamic pricing model.
Assuming compensating actions can reverse physical preparation or a completed delivery.

200,000 active couriers report location every five seconds.

estimates.calculation: 1,000,000 / 86,400 = 11.6 orders/s average; 20x peak is about 232/s.
estimates.implication: Order correctness is more important than extreme write sharding at this scale. Each order creates multiple downstream commands and events.

estimates.label: Courier telemetry
estimates.calculation: 200,000 / 5 = 40,000 location updates/s.
estimates.implication: Isolate location ingestion from transactional order storage. Reuse a geographic candidate index and an authoritative dispatch reservation path.

api.purpose: Validate quote expiry, persist an idempotent order, and start the workflow. Never trust client-calculated totals.
Authenticate the merchant and conditionally accept or reject only the expected order state.
Apply the cancellation policy for the current stage, schedule compensations, and expose pending refund or manual-review states.

dataModel.notes: Persist step progress and retries so a worker restart resumes rather than repeats untracked side effects.

flows.name: Place and fulfill an order
steps: Validate the server-side quote and persist the immutable order snapshot and workflow start event.
Authorize payment and request merchant acceptance using idempotent commands with deadlines. The exact ordering depends on commercial policy.
Reserve a courier near the expected ready time, not necessarily at order creation; keep dispatch retries separate from payment retries.
Persist pickup and delivery transitions, then capture or finalize payment at the policy-defined stage and notify participants through committed events.

flows.name: Compensate a failed order
steps: Identify the last committed workflow state after a rejection, timeout, or cancellation request.
Cancel unneeded courier reservations, release inventory where supported, and void payment authorization or request a refund as appropriate.
Track compensation commands durably and retry idempotently; a failed refund remains visible as pending, not falsely complete.
Escalate irreversible or ambiguous cases, such as already prepared food, captured funds, or a disputed delivery, to a defined support workflow.

decisions.choice: Use an explicit orchestrator for the multi-party order lifecycle and its deadlines.
decisions.tradeOff: It centralizes workflow visibility but requires careful versioning and recovery. Pure event choreography reduces a central coordinator but can hide cyclic dependencies and compensation state.

decisions.choice: Separate authorization from capture when the provider and business flow support it.
decisions.tradeOff: A hold can expire and capture can fail later. Capturing immediately simplifies one step but increases refunds after merchant rejection.

decisions.choice: Match couriers against a predicted preparation time and update the plan as the order evolves.
decisions.tradeOff: Early dispatch increases courier waiting; late dispatch increases food waiting. ETA accuracy and uncertainty should influence the offer policy.

failureModes.scenario: The merchant accepts after the customer cancellation has committed.
failureModes.handling: Check order state/version before accepting the event. Reject stale transitions and apply the policy for any physical preparation already begun.

failureModes.scenario: Payment authorization succeeds but the workflow worker crashes.
failureModes.handling: Retry the same command ID and reconcile with the provider instead of generating a new authorization. Persist ambiguous results until resolved.

failureModes.scenario: A courier disappears after pickup.
failureModes.handling: Use telemetry freshness, deadlines, support escalation, and customer communication. Monitor stage age, compensation backlog, authorization expiry, dispatch latency, and failed terminal transitions.

selfCheck.question: Why is a saga not the same as rolling back a database transaction?
selfCheck.answer: Each participant may have already committed independent or physical effects. A saga performs new compensating actions, such as refunds or reservation releases, which can themselves fail and may not restore the exact original world.

selfCheck.question: Why store an item and price snapshot on the order?
selfCheck.answer: Menus, taxes, availability, and promotions can change while an order is processed. The stored snapshot records the agreement the customer accepted and supports consistent fulfillment, disputes, refunds, and auditing.

selfCheck.question: What should the UI show when cancellation succeeded but the refund is still pending?
selfCheck.answer: Expose those as separate states: the order is canceled and the refund is pending or under review. Marking the entire workflow complete would hide an unresolved financial obligation and make recovery or customer support harder.

design-video-streaming-platform.summary: Design an on-demand video platform with independent upload, processing, and playback paths. Store media in object storage and deliver immutable segments through a CDN; application servers manage metadata and authorization rather than proxying every video byte. Processing must tolerate retries and only publish manifests that reference complete playable assets.
clarifyingQuestions: Is the core user-generated on-demand video, or also live streaming and licensed subscription content?
Which processing and moderation steps must complete before playback is allowed?
What are upload limits, processing-time objectives, privacy controls, and retention requirements for source and derived media?

deepDives.title: Untrusted uploads and versioned processing jobs
paragraphs: Issue a scoped upload session and send bytes directly to object storage, keeping source media quarantined until validation completes. Confirm storage state and ownership server-side; an upload notification is not evidence that the media is safe, within quota, or ready to publish.

Treat probing, transcoding, thumbnail generation, captions, and moderation as a retryable workflow. A job identity and unique video/source/profile-version tuple prevent duplicate retries from creating unrelated assets. Bound parser CPU, memory, and duration, and classify permanently malformed input so it does not consume the queue forever.

A creator can delete a video while an old worker still runs. Every publication step must verify the current video generation and tombstone state before advertising output. Immutable rendition paths plus conditional state changes prevent a late successful worker from resurrecting removed or superseded content.
deepDives.invariant: Only the current authorized non-deleted source generation may publish validated media; processing retries cannot resurrect an obsolete video.

followUp.question: What stops a transcoder from republishing a video after its creator deletes it?
followUp.answer: The final publication transaction checks the current video generation and deletion state. A completed worker task is not enough. Retain tombstones or version fences so a stale worker's output remains unreferenced and can be reclaimed safely.

deepDives.title: Playable readiness and CDN economics
paragraphs: Define a minimum playable set, such as compatible baseline video plus required audio, before marking a video ready. Higher-quality renditions can become available later through a new compatible manifest version. Do not advertise every planned quality while some segments are still missing.

Aligned keyframes, segment boundaries, and immutable URLs let players adapt bitrate without crossing incompatible timelines. Application APIs authorize and locate media; CDNs serve the bytes. Seek and resume behavior relies on the streaming protocol or bounded range requests, not on downloading the entire source file again.

Long-tail user-generated videos differ from a small predictable premiere catalog. Warm popular content where demand supports it, use origin shielding, and measure byte hit rate rather than only request hit rate. Many cached thumbnails can make request metrics look healthy while large uncached videos still saturate origin bandwidth.
deepDives.invariant: A ready manifest references a complete supported playback baseline, and cached content remains tied to its immutable media version.

followUp.question: Why can a high CDN request hit rate hide an expensive origin problem?
followUp.answer: Small images or metadata may dominate request counts while large video segments miss. Measure byte hit rate, origin egress, and per-rendition demand so the cache metric reflects the bandwidth and cost that matter.

deepDives.title: Processing fairness, privacy, and retention
paragraphs: Long high-resolution uploads consume far more processing than short clips. Schedule by estimated work and account budgets, cap concurrent jobs, and preserve capacity for small uploads. Autoscaling on job count alone can underreact to a few enormous files or overreact to many cheap tasks.

Private and unlisted have different meanings: an unguessable link may be shareable, while private playback needs authorization. Apply policy at metadata and delivery boundaries and define takedown propagation. A public video made private cannot retract already downloaded copies, but future access must follow the new policy within its documented bound.

Separate retention for source media, published renditions, failed temporary output, and audit metadata. Keep assets referenced by supported manifests and reclaim abandoned jobs only after a safe recovery window. Codec migrations and policy changes need staged publication and rollback without prematurely deleting the last playable version.
deepDives.invariant: Processing load cannot bypass account budgets or visibility policy, and retention never removes the only asset version still promised to active playback.

followUp.question: Should every upload receive the same scheduling weight?
followUp.answer: No. Duration, resolution, codec, and required renditions change processing cost dramatically. Estimate work, impose per-account budgets, and monitor waiting time by workload class so large creators do not starve ordinary uploads.

signals.name: Upload-to-ready latency
signals.measure: Track queue and processing time by duration, codec, resolution, and account cohort.
signals.response: Isolate expensive or malformed workloads and scale measured processing capacity with fairness limits.

signals.name: Playback and bandwidth
signals.measure: Measure startup, rebuffering, missing segments, byte hit rate, and origin egress by rendition.
signals.response: Roll back broken publication versions, shield origins, and prioritize useful renditions.

signals.name: Lifecycle safety
signals.measure: Track stale-worker publication rejections, tombstone propagation, orphaned bytes, and retained-manifest references.
signals.response: Stop unsafe cleanup or publication and reconcile object inventory with authoritative metadata.

security: Isolate media parsing/transcoding, verify ownership and size limits, and protect direct-upload capabilities from cross-account reuse.
Enforce private playback and creator authorization independently of knowledge of a video URL; audit moderation overrides.
Minimize sensitive metadata and protect takedown/deletion propagation across search, recommendations, and media delivery.
validation: Crash and retry every processing stage, delete videos mid-job, and verify generation checks prevent stale publication.
Validate manifests against real compatible test assets, including audio, captions, seeks, and bitrate switches before promoting a profile version.
Load-test heterogeneous uploads and cold-origin playback, then canary codec and retention migrations with a playable rollback version.

prerequisites: Object storage, signed URLs, CDNs, and cache control
Transcoding, adaptive bitrate streaming, and background jobs

functional: Upload large videos resumably and track processing status.
Transcode into several renditions and serve adaptive-bitrate playback.
Enforce visibility, support deletion, and retain basic metadata and watch progress.
nonFunctional: Illustrative target: playback starts within two seconds under the defined network conditions.
Keep playback available during isolated processing or metadata-service failures where cached authorization permits.
Recover partial uploads and processing jobs without publishing broken videos.
outOfScope: Live streaming, real-time chat, and a full recommendation engine.
Treating signed URLs alone as DRM or a guarantee against copying content.

assumptions: 10 million daily viewers watch 30 minutes/day at an average 3 Mbit/s.
100,000 uploads/day, each ten minutes at a 10 Mbit/s source bitrate.

estimates.label: Playback bandwidth
estimates.calculation: 10,000,000 x 1,800 s x 3,000,000 bit/s / 8 = 6.75 PB/day, or 625 Gbit/s average.
estimates.implication: CDN hit ratio and egress dominate the media path. Peak demand and regional distribution matter more than raw API request count.

estimates.label: Source uploads
estimates.calculation: 100,000 x 600 s x 10,000,000 bit/s / 8 = 75 TB/day of source video.
estimates.implication: Multiple renditions, replication, thumbnails, and retention increase storage. Use lifecycle policies and cost-aware encoding tiers.

api.purpose: Create an authorized upload session with multipart targets, size limits, and expiry; do not proxy the full upload through the metadata API.
Verify object completion, persist processing state, and enqueue idempotent processing for a specific source version.
Check visibility and return a current manifest URL or short-lived access token only when assets are playable.

dataModel.fields: videoId, ownerId, title, visibility, sourceVersion, processingState, manifestVersion
dataModel.notes: Model uploaded, processing, ready, failed, and deleted states. A successful upload is not equivalent to playable media.

dataModel.fields: videoId, sourceVersion, codec, resolution, bitrate, objectPrefix, status
dataModel.notes: Use immutable versioned object paths so stale CDN entries cannot mix old and new segments.

dataModel.fields: jobId, sourceVersion, rendition, attempt, leaseVersion, checkpoint
dataModel.notes: Stable job identity and fenced ownership prevent duplicate workers from publishing conflicting outputs.

architecture.diagram:
flowchart TD
 Creator[Creator app] --> API[Upload and metadata API]
 API --> Metadata[(Video metadata)]
 Creator -->|signed multipart upload| Source[(Source object storage)]
 Source --> Queue[Processing jobs]
 Queue --> Workers[Transcode and validate]
 Workers --> Media[(Immutable segments and manifests)]
 Workers -->|publish ready version| Metadata
 Viewer[Viewer] -->|authorize playback| API
 Viewer -->|manifest and segments| CDN[CDN]
 CDN -->|cache miss| Media

flows.name: Upload and publish
steps: Issue a bounded resumable upload session and let the client send parts directly to object storage.
Verify completion and checksum, validate the file, and enqueue source-versioned processing jobs.
Workers transcode and segment into immutable rendition paths, validate output, and retry failed chunks idempotently.
Publish a manifest and atomically mark a playable version ready only after its referenced assets exist. Additional renditions can be published as later manifest versions.

flows.name: Play and adapt
steps: Authorize the viewer against current visibility and return a manifest URL with the appropriate access policy.
The player fetches the manifest and segments from the CDN, selecting a rendition based on bandwidth and buffer state.
On cache miss, the CDN fetches immutable segments from origin; origin shielding and prewarming help with sudden popular releases.
Record quality-of-experience signals and watch progress asynchronously. Deletion requires a defined revocation window across tokens and CDN caches.

decisions.choice: Generate a rendition ladder and use HLS or DASH manifests to let the player adapt.
decisions.tradeOff: More renditions improve fit for devices and networks but cost encoding time and storage. Segment length trades request overhead against startup and switching speed.

decisions.choice: Precompute common renditions and add expensive formats selectively.
decisions.tradeOff: Encoding everything wastes resources on unwatched uploads; on-demand encoding can hurt first-viewer latency. Use a popularity and device-support policy.

decisions.choice: Use authenticated playback setup with short-lived signed access and CDN-compatible caching.
decisions.tradeOff: Tokens can remain valid after access changes until expiry. Strict revocation and DRM requirements need additional mechanisms and may reduce cache efficiency.

failureModes.scenario: A transcoder crashes halfway through a rendition.
failureModes.handling: Resume or retry an idempotent source-versioned job, keep partial outputs unpublished, and garbage-collect abandoned artifacts.

failureModes.scenario: A popular video overwhelms the origin on a cold CDN.
failureModes.handling: Use origin shielding, request coalescing, cacheable immutable paths, and selective prewarming; reserve origin capacity for cache misses.

failureModes.scenario: A manifest references missing or inaccessible segments.
failureModes.handling: Validate assets before publishing and retain a last-known playable version. Monitor startup delay, rebuffer ratio, segment errors, CDN hit rate, and processing backlog.

selfCheck.question: Why should application servers avoid proxying all video traffic?
selfCheck.answer: Media bandwidth dwarfs metadata API traffic and is well suited to object storage plus CDN caching. Proxying every byte through application servers increases cost, connection pressure, and failure coupling without adding necessary business logic to each segment request.

selfCheck.question: When is a video ready to publish?
selfCheck.answer: At least one valid playable rendition and its manifest must be complete, accessible, and consistent with the metadata state. Upload completion alone is insufficient; publishing a manifest before its segments exist produces playback failures.

selfCheck.question: Does deleting the metadata row instantly revoke every copy of a video?
selfCheck.answer: No. CDN caches, previously issued tokens, browser buffers, and downloaded copies have separate lifetimes. Define a practical revocation window, purge or version assets as needed, and do not promise control over copies already delivered to a viewer.

design-payment-system.summary: Design payment orchestration around an external processor with a durable internal ledger and reconciliation. A network timeout is an unknown outcome, not proof of failure. Separate payment intent, provider attempts, and accounting entries so retries, callbacks, refunds, and settlement reports can be reconciled without inventing money or charging twice.
clarifyingQuestions: Are we orchestrating a processor, maintaining a wallet ledger, or also performing settlement and payouts?
When are authorization, capture, refund, dispute, and currency conversion supported?
What are the provider's idempotency window, outcome-lookup capability, callback semantics, and reconciliation source?

deepDives.title: Payment intent, attempts, and unknown outcomes
paragraphs: Separate the customer's logical payment intent from each provider attempt. Persist the attempt UUID, request hash, provider key, and legal starting state before making the external call. Scope client idempotency to the merchant or owner, and reject reuse of a key with a different amount, currency, or purpose.

A timeout can occur after the provider commits. Keep the attempt unknown and query or retry it using the same supported provider identity. Creating a new key or switching processors immediately can charge twice because deduplication at one provider does not coordinate with another.

Provider idempotency may have a limited retention window. Do not blindly replay an old request after that window expires; use lookup, settlement evidence, or an explicit exception workflow. Fence concurrent workers handling the same attempt and resolve synchronous responses and verified callbacks through one durable state machine.
deepDives.invariant: An unresolved attempt is not replaced with a fresh external charge identity merely because its network response was lost.

followUp.question: Why is automatic failover to a second processor dangerous after a timeout?
followUp.answer: The first processor may already have charged the customer, and the second has no shared deduplication state. Reconcile the first attempt or follow an explicit risk policy before creating a new attempt elsewhere; high availability does not remove outcome uncertainty.

deepDives.title: Immutable balanced accounting
paragraphs: Record financial movements as balanced ledger transactions with immutable entries. Debits and credits balance within each currency and accounting boundary; summing unrelated currencies is meaningless. Use integer minor units or fixed-precision amounts with explicit rounding, not binary floating-point arithmetic for money.

A displayed balance can be a projection, but posting entries and required balance constraints must be enforced atomically by the ledger authority. Keep transaction UUIDs and unique external references to prevent duplicate posting. Concurrency control is required when spending against the same account, even if the overall payment rate is modest.

Refunds, fees, disputes, and corrections are new postings linked to the original obligation rather than edits that erase history. Currency conversion needs explicit rates and balancing accounts. A successful provider charge is an input to accounting, not permission to mutate arbitrary account totals without a traceable ledger transaction.
deepDives.invariant: Every committed ledger transaction balances in its defined currency boundary and can be linked to an immutable, uniquely applied business obligation.

followUp.question: Why not fix a wrong balance by editing the account total?
followUp.answer: It destroys the evidence connecting the balance to its transactions and makes reconciliation unreliable. Post an authorized correcting transaction with a reason and references, then rebuild or update the balance projection from the ledger.

deepDives.title: Callbacks, settlement, and financial recovery
paragraphs: Callbacks can be duplicated, reordered, or delayed. Verify signatures and expected financial details, deduplicate provider events, and enforce legal transitions. A late authorization event must not overwrite a refund or dispute state merely because it arrived last.

Commit ledger or payment transitions together with an outbox for downstream work. A consumer can then retry fulfillment or notification idempotently. This does not make the processor and database one transaction; retain recovery scans for stalled attempts and durable compensation for failed external actions.

Reconcile internal attempts and ledger postings against provider transaction lookup and settlement reports. Distinguish processor acceptance from actual settlement, fees, chargebacks, and payout. Track discrepancies to resolution with controlled operator actions; a system can return very few HTTP errors while silently accumulating financial exceptions.
deepDives.invariant: Duplicate or late provider evidence cannot post money twice or overwrite a legal later financial state without an explicit reconciled transition.

followUp.question: Why is reconciliation required when callbacks are retried reliably?
followUp.answer: Callbacks still reflect only part of the lifecycle and can be misconfigured, delayed, or interpreted incorrectly. Settlement adds fees, reversals, and timing differences. Independent comparison with provider evidence detects omissions and ledger mismatches that request success metrics miss.

signals.name: Unknown and stuck attempts
signals.measure: Track age by provider/state, lookup failures, and attempts approaching the provider idempotency expiry.
signals.response: Reconcile before replaying, fence duplicate workers, and expose pending status rather than inventing failure.

signals.name: Ledger invariants
signals.measure: Alert on unbalanced postings, duplicate external references, and projection-to-ledger discrepancies.
signals.response: Stop unsafe posting and repair through audited corrective transactions, not direct balance edits.

signals.name: Settlement completeness
signals.measure: Track unmatched settlements, fees, refunds, chargebacks, and unapplied outbox events.
signals.response: Assign discrepancies to a durable recovery workflow and reconcile before releasing affected obligations.

security: Use processor tokens and minimize card-data scope; tokenization does not remove all payment-security or compliance obligations.
Authorize merchant/account actions and recompute trusted amounts; verify callback signatures, currency, amount, and provider identity.
Restrict refund, payout, and ledger-correction permissions, protect secrets and audit logs, and apply dual review where financial policy requires it.
validation: Inject failures before and after provider calls, persist/replay callbacks, and assert one logical financial effect per supported attempt identity.
Use property checks for per-currency ledger balance, duplicate posting, concurrent spending, refunds, fees, and precision boundaries.
Rehearse settlement reconciliation and idempotency-window expiry; canary processor/schema changes with audited rollback and unresolved-attempt tracking.

prerequisites: ACID transactions, unique constraints, and durable idempotency
Payment authorization/capture, double-entry accounting, and reconciliation

functional: Create a payment intent and authorize/capture it using tokenized payment details.
Handle retries, provider callbacks, cancellations, and partial or full refunds.
Record balanced accounting entries and reconcile internal state with provider and settlement reports.
nonFunctional: Do not duplicate a logical charge when requests or workers retry.
Preserve auditable state changes and balanced ledger postings per currency.
Expose pending and unknown outcomes honestly while recovering from provider or database failures.
outOfScope: Building a card network or storing raw card numbers in application tables.
Treating this interview design as a complete compliance, fraud, or production accounting specification.

assumptions: 10 million payment attempts/day with a 10x peak.
Assume at least four 200-byte ledger entry records per completed flow; real fees, refunds, and settlement entries add more.

estimates.label: Payment throughput
estimates.calculation: 10,000,000 / 86,400 = 116 attempts/s average; 10x peak is about 1,160/s.
estimates.implication: Correctness, provider limits, and tail latency dominate before exotic sharding. Isolate slow provider calls from database transaction locks.

estimates.label: Ledger payload
estimates.calculation: 10,000,000 x 4 x 200 B = 8 GB/day raw ledger-entry payload.
estimates.implication: Indexes, immutable audit history, provider responses, replicas, and retention increase storage. Preserve auditability instead of overwriting history to save space.

api.purpose: Require a merchant-scoped Idempotency-Key and request hash. Persist a stable intent and return the original result for an identical retry.
Create one logical capture command for the permitted amount. Reuse a stable provider idempotency key and enforce the current intent state.
Idempotently reserve/refund a bounded amount without exceeding captured funds after prior refunds, using transactional checks.
Verify signatures and replay protection, deduplicate events, and process state changes asynchronously from durable receipt.

dataModel.fields: intentId, merchantId, orderId, amountMinor, currency, state, version
dataModel.notes: Use integer minor units and a currency definition, not floating-point money. Authorization, capture, settlement, and refund are separate states.

dataModel.fields: attemptId, intentId, operation, providerKey, providerReference, outcome
dataModel.notes: Keep pending/unknown outcomes and the stable provider idempotency key. Never generate a fresh key merely because an HTTP response timed out.

dataModel.fields: transactionId, businessEventId, accountId, currency, signedAmountMinor
dataModel.notes: Post balanced entries atomically: signed amounts sum to zero within each currency. Enforce unique business events; correct mistakes with new reversing entries, not edits.

dataModel.fields: merchantId, key, requestHash, resourceId, storedResponse
dataModel.notes: Bind the key to the operation and request payload. Retention must cover the promised retry window, and concurrent first requests need uniqueness enforcement.

architecture.diagram:
flowchart TD
 Merchant[Merchant client] --> API[Idempotent payment API]
 API --> Store[(Intents attempts and outbox)]
 Store --> Worker[Payment worker]
 Worker -->|stable provider key| PSP[Payment processor]
 PSP --> Webhook[Verified callback intake]
 Webhook --> Transition[Idempotent state transition]
 Worker --> Transition
 Transition --> Ledger[(Balanced ledger and event uniqueness)]
 PSP --> Reports[Settlement reports and status lookup]
 Reports --> Reconcile[Reconciliation worker]
 Reconcile --> Transition

flows.name: Create and execute a payment
steps: Validate the server-owned amount and currency, reserve the idempotency key, and persist the intent plus an outbox command atomically.
A worker records a stable provider key and calls the processor outside a long-held database transaction.
Apply the provider outcome through a versioned, idempotent state transition. Post the relevant ledger transaction and an outbox event atomically inside the owned database boundary.
Return or expose pending status for unknown outcomes. Provider success followed by an internal database failure is repaired through retry, callback, or reconciliation, not a second charge.

flows.name: Reconcile and refund
steps: Persist and authenticate callbacks, deduplicate event IDs, and tolerate out-of-order events without regressing a captured payment to merely authorized.
Query ambiguous attempts by provider reference/key and compare internal records with settlement reports.
For a refund, transactionally check remaining refundable amount, create a unique refund command, and track its external outcome.
Post new balanced accounting entries for confirmed refunds or adjustments. Route unresolved differences to an auditable exception queue with ownership and deadlines.

decisions.choice: Keep owned state, ledger postings, and outbox records atomic where they share a database.
decisions.tradeOff: The external processor is not part of that transaction. Idempotency plus reconciliation bridges the gap; holding a database lock during the HTTP call does not make it atomic.

decisions.choice: Keep an append-only journal and derive or transactionally maintain balances from committed entries.
decisions.tradeOff: A balanced ledger prevents certain accounting errors but does not prove the provider moved money correctly. Reconcile external reality separately.

decisions.choice: Prefer pending/unknown states and safe retries over guessing that a timed-out payment failed.
decisions.tradeOff: Customers may wait longer for a final answer, but retrying with a new identity risks duplicate charges and costly remediation.

failureModes.scenario: The processor captures funds but its response is lost.
failureModes.handling: Reuse the same provider idempotency key, inspect status, and wait for authenticated callbacks or reconciliation. Do not immediately try another processor.

failureModes.scenario: Two concurrent refund requests exceed the remaining captured amount.
failureModes.handling: Reserve refundable funds under a transaction or conditional update with the required isolation, and deduplicate each refund operation before calling the provider.

failureModes.scenario: Callbacks are forged, duplicated, or reordered.
failureModes.handling: Verify signatures on the expected raw payload, enforce replay controls, deduplicate IDs, and validate legal state transitions. Monitor unknown-attempt age, ledger imbalance, duplicate suppression, and reconciliation backlog.

selfCheck.question: What should happen after a capture request times out?
selfCheck.answer: Treat the result as unknown. Retry using the same provider-supported idempotency key or query the existing attempt, then reconcile with callbacks or reports. A new key or immediate processor failover may charge the customer again.

selfCheck.question: Why does a local unique payment row not guarantee exactly-once charging?
selfCheck.answer: The external processor's side effect and your local commit are separate operations. A worker can crash after the charge but before recording success, so retries need provider-side idempotency and a reconciliation path in addition to local uniqueness.

selfCheck.question: Does a balanced double-entry ledger prove a payment settled?
selfCheck.answer: No. It proves an internal accounting invariant, not that the provider transferred funds. Provider references, settlement reports, and reconciliation must verify the external outcome; adjustments remain new auditable ledger entries.
